Stiff person syndrome does not always
occur with maternal passive transfer
of GAD65 antibodies
R. Nemni, MD; L.M. Caniatti, MD; M. Gironi, MD; E. Bazzigaluppi, BD; and D. De Grandis, MD
Abstract—The authors report the presence of high titer antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD65) until age
24 months in two asymptomatic newborns of a woman with stiff-person syndrome (SPS). No signs of SPS were detectable
in the two children at ages 6 and 8 years. This observation indicates that other cofactors are involved in the pathogenesis
of SPS.
NEUROLOGY 2004;62:2101–2102
Autoantibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-
GAD65) in serum and CSF of a patient with stiff-
person syndrome (SPS), epilepsy, and type 1 diabetes
mellitus (DM) were detected in 1988.
1 A high concen-
tration of GAD and /H9253-aminobutyric acid (GABA) was
found in pancreatic /H9252-cells, male germ cells, oviduct,
and ovary, suggesting a possible pathogenic link be-
tween diseases affecting neural and non-neural
GABA systems, such as SPS, epilepsy, DM, and poly-
endocrine autoimmunity. Studies conducted on a
large series of patients demonstrated a high preva-
lence (60%) of anti-GAD65 in SPS.
2 Anti-GAD65 was
subsequently found in patients with late-onset cere-
bellar ataxia
3 and syndromes thought to be caused
by the impairment of the inhibitory GABAergic neu-
rotransmission from the cerebellum to the inferior
olivary nuclei, such as palatal myoclonus and down-
beat nystagmus.
4,5 The possibility of detecting anti-
GAD65 in different diseases suggests that it may
have different specificity and pathogenicity and that
multiple coexisting factors are probably required to
develop the clinical syndromes. We report a typical
case of SPS and epilepsy with anti-GAD65 in a
woman who delivered two unaffected newborns with
high titer anti-GAD65.
Patients and methods. Patient history. A woman aged 31
years with an uneventful family and medical history developed a
slowly progressive stiffness and rigidity in axial muscles 10 years
earlier. She had painful muscle spasms triggered by tactile and
emotional stimuli, partial complex seizures, and paroxysmal auto-
nomic dysfunction with tachycardia, hyperidrosis, and itch at-
tacks. Clinical examination showed hyperlordosis of the lumbar
spine. The muscular tone was markedly increased in the paraspi-
nal region and proximally in the lower limbs. Spontaneous and
touch-sensitive flexor spasms of the arms and legs were present.
Deep tendon reflexes were normal and symmetric with flexor
plantar responses. An EMG showed continuous electric activity at
rest in the thoracoabdominal muscles. SPS was then diagnosed,
and diazepam treatment was started (50 mg/d) with temporary
response. Subsequent progression of the disease to the lower limbs
hampered the gait. After a good response to baclofen treatment,
she became pregnant. All drugs were discontinued with a subse-
quent clinical deterioration.
At the 20th week of pregnancy, a sample of amnion and blood
from the funiculus was taken, and anti-GAD65 was detected in
the amniotic fluid and fetal and maternal serum. At the 39th
week, the newborn was delivered by cesarean section. Clinical and
neurologic examinations of the newborn were normal. A week
after delivery, drugs were successfully started again. Two years
later, the patient entered her second pregnancy, and treatment
was discontinued. Although she worsened, she delivered a second
healthy newborn at the 40th week.

High titer of anti-GAD65 was evident in the two infants until
age 24 months (table), but no signs of SPS or other anti-GAD-
related diseases were detected at 6- and 8-year follow-up
evaluations.
Methods. The presence of anti-GAD65 was detected by an
immunoprecipitation assay of 35S-methionine-labeled, in vitro-
translated, full-length recombinant human GAD65.
4,6
Results. The profile of anti-GAD65 in the mother and
two newborns is summarized in the table. Sera from 86
blood donors were negative in all assays.
Discussion. Several neurologic and non-neurologic
syndromes have been related to the presence of anti-
GAD65. A study investigating the prevalence of anti-
GAD65 in 301 neurologic patients pointed out that
anti-GAD65 was present in patients with SPS with
high prevalence (81.8%) and high value (120 U) but
with a much lower prevalence (6.5%) and lower value
(31 U) in patients with other neurologic diseases.
2 In
SPS, anti-GAD65 is not considered a simple nonspe-
cific epiphenomenon of neurologic damage or a by-
stander reaction to an autoimmune process. It has
been hypothesized that anti-GAD65 exerts its patho-
genetic action on GABAergic neurons by altering mo-
tor unit activity in the spinal cord. We describe two
offspring of a woman affected by SPS, bearing high

titer anti-GAD65 up to 24 months without any clini-
cal sign of the disease. This observation, along with
data reporting the presence of circulating anti-
GAD65 in healthy control subjects and of patients
with SPS without anti-GAD65 (up to 40%), suggests
cofactors in the pathogenesis of the disease. We offer
explanations of the failure of this “natural passive
transfer.” The putative cognate antigen of anti-
GAD65 is retained inside CNS, a secluded organ
where access of anti-GAD65 is restricted. In the two
infants, the integrity of the blood –brain barrier
(BBB) is supposed to prevent the passage of anti-
GAD65 into the CNS. The role played by the BBB
integrity in preventing the potential pathogenicity of
anti-GAD65 is well documented. Two years after al-
logenic bone marrow transplantation, a patient de-
veloped intractable myoclonus after head trauma.
7
The patient had high titer serum antibodies to gluta-
mate receptor 3, and autopsy revealed that these
antibodies bound to patient ’s CNS structures, pro-
viding evidence for their pathogenetic role. The same
antibodies were also present in the donor ’s serum,
which was negative for any clinical signs of myoclo-
nus up to 3-year follow-up evaluation. It is possible
that the leakage of BBB, caused by head trauma,
turned the potential pathogenicity of these antibod-
ies into an autoimmune disease.
Other immunogenetic factors could explain the in-
fants’ resistance to the disease. The capacity of an
autoantibody to trigger autoimmune response is re-
lated to the presence of a loop whereby the autoreac-
tive T cells and B cells mutually and sequentially
stimulate each other. Human leukocyte antigen phe-
notypes, cytokine milieu (different in adults and
newborns), and immunocompetent T cells can pre-
vent anti-GAD65 pathogenicity. In another study,
maternal ovarian epitope-specific autoantibodies
transmitted to progeny have been shown to induce a
de novo T-cell response in neonatal mice.
8 These au-
toantibodies, nonpathogenic in adults, triggered a
T-cell response only in the progeny, leading to a se-
vere organ-specific autoimmune disease. The disease
was prevented if the mice were not fed with breast
milk of the mother. We report the same results in
these infants, who were not breast-fed. Therefore,
epitope-specific autoantibodies could trigger an auto-
immune disease only if an interaction through differ-
ent immune mediators is orchestrated.
We also found the persistence of the high titer
serum anti-GAD65 in the two newborns. We were
unable to define whether it was caused by an abnor-
mal persistence of maternal antibodies only or by a
true transient neonatal autoimmunity. Previously,
the persistence of anti-GAD65 /H1102224 months after
birth has been reported in offspring committed to
develop insulin-dependent DM.
6
We conclude that offspring of women with SPS
can bear high titer anti-GAD65 up to age 24 months
with no signs of anti-GAD-related disease at 6- and
8-year follow-up evaluation.
